identification.summary: Ababil of Minab is a pro-Iran persona that claimed a March 2026 cyberattack on the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (LA Metro), including administrative access to its VMware vCenter environment and a related attack on GPS service provider Vyncs [S1]. Israeli firm Gambit Security assesses it is not a standalone hacktivist crew but is tied to Black Shadow and Iran's MOIS [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: 2026-03: LA Metro detected the intrusion around 16 March 2026, and the persona claimed it online about two weeks later [S2][S1]. Public reporting before this incident was not found.
identification.notes: The name refers to a US strike on a girls' school in Minab, Iran [S1][S2]. Dataminr cautioned that a definitive capability or intent assessment was premature [S1]. Gambit's MOIS/Black Shadow linkage is a vendor assessment; see attribution and gaps [S2][S3]. No Microsoft name or MITRE group ID was found for this persona.

attribution.sponsor: Gambit Security (Israel) assesses the group is tied to Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) via Black Shadow infrastructure [S2][S3]. No government attribution of this specific incident was found.
attribution.confidence: Contested. Gambit states the group is not a new standalone hacktivist crew as it claims [S2]. ClearSky and Israel's National Cyber Directorate are cited as linking the infrastructure to Black Shadow, which Israel attributes to MOIS [S3]. LA Metro said attribution is part of the investigation and it would not speculate [S2]. Dataminr called definitive assessment premature [S1].
attribution.basis: Gambit forensic analysis of the intrusion and infrastructure overlap with Black Shadow [S2][S3]; ClearSky separate work [S3]. These are vendor findings, not government attribution.

objectives: The persona's messaging is pro-Iran and framed around retaliation for the Minab school strike [S1]. Gambit assesses the activity is state-directed with a hacktivist cover, combining data theft and destruction [S2][S3]. Specific operator intent is not confirmed.

sectors: Regional transit (South Florida Regional Transportation Authority)
regions: Israel, Saudi Arabia and Turkey (victims identified by Gambit)
targeting.notes: Gambit reports the wider campaign hit SFRTA, UNIMAC and Vyncs besides LA Metro, with victims also in Israel, Saudi Arabia and Turkey [S3]. LA Metro said train and bus circulation was not interrupted; internal systems were taken down, affecting fare reloads and arrival signs [S1][S2].

capabilities.summary: The persona claimed administrative access to LA Metro's VMware vCenter environment [S1]. Gambit reports attackers deleted virtual machines, used backup software to wipe disks, and stole at least 700 GB of emails, backups and other files [S3][S2]. Gambit also reports the group used ChatGPT to refine a Python script that enumerated and dropped databases in the Vyncs environment [S3]. The group claimed 500 TB wiped and 1 TB exfiltrated; LA Metro confirmed partial access but did not validate those volumes [S2][S5].

campaigns.name: LA Metro intrusion
campaigns.summary: LA Metro detected a breach around mid-March 2026; internal systems were taken down, with delays to fare-card reloads and non-operational arrival signs, but no interruption to rail or bus service [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Public claim of LA Metro and Vyncs attacks
campaigns.summary: Ababil of Minab claimed the LA Metro attack (vCenter admin access) and an attack on Vyncs, and alleged 500 TB wiped and 1 TB exfiltrated [S1][S5].

campaigns.name: LA Metro confirms breach
campaigns.summary: Reporting states LA Metro confirmed the breach on 2 April 2026; one report says it had not confirmed as of 15 April, so reporting is inconsistent [S3][S1].

campaigns.name: Gambit Security attribution report
campaigns.summary: Gambit publishes findings tying the activity to Black Shadow/MOIS and identifying further victims including SFRTA, UNIMAC and Vyncs [S2][S3][S4].

diamond.adversary: Pro-Iran persona; Gambit assesses MOIS-linked operators behind it [S2][S3].
diamond.capability: vCenter-level access, VM deletion, disk wiping via backup software, bulk data theft, AI-assisted database-dropping script [S1][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Overlap with Black Shadow infrastructure per Gambit and ClearSky; specific indicators not obtained [S3].
diamond.victim: LA Metro, SFRTA, UNIMAC, Vyncs; further victims in Israel, Saudi Arabia, Turkey [S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Persona branding invokes the Minab school strike as a grievance narrative [S1][S2].
diamond.technology: Virtualization management (VMware vCenter), backup systems and database environments at transit and tracking-service providers [S1][S3].

gaps: Primary Gambit Security report and ClearSky report were not opened; findings rely on press coverage (TechCrunch, Security Boulevard, Route Fifty, Reuters via i24).
WebFetch failed (host resolution) for TechCrunch, SecurityAffairs, Dataminr and The Record, so article details come from search-result summaries only.
Initial access vector and specific malware are not public in the sources gathered.
Some search summaries describe Black Shadow as also tracked as Static Kitten/MuddyWater; this was not verified and may conflate vendor clusters. Do not merge until confirmed in a primary source.
Claimed volumes (500 TB wiped) are unverified; reported dates conflict (confirmation 2 April vs not confirmed as of 15 April).
No Microsoft actor name, MITRE group ID or government attribution located.
Security Affairs piece is opinion-style analysis; treat as commentary.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Virtualization management (vCenter), backup platforms and database servers at transit and logistics providers are key terrain; public transit is a visible, non-DoD civilian target [S1][S3]. STEP 2: The persona gives plausible deniability and a grievance narrative, which may lower the threshold for destructive action against US civil infrastructure [S2]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is administrative access to virtualization, deletion of VMs, wiping via backup tooling, and bulk theft, followed by a public Telegram-style claim [S1][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is further wiper/theft intrusions against US and regional civil operators of modest hardening, with inflated claims. MDCOA is destructive access to a provider with DoD or installation transport/logistics ties timed to US-Iran escalation. Candidate indicators: unusual vCenter admin logins, mass VM deletions, backup software issuing disk-wipe jobs, large mail/backup exfiltration, and database-drop scripts [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track claims by Iran-aligned personas but separate claims from verified impact, since volume claims were unverified [S5]. (2) Authorities: incidents at civilian operators sit outside DoD networks, so coordination runs through CISA/FBI and DC3 for DIB-linked suppliers; Gambit's attribution is not government attribution [S2]. (3) Mission assurance: harden and back up offline virtualization management and backup systems for installation-supporting services, and plan for loss of internal systems with continued physical operations, as LA Metro experienced [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with commercial providers and partners in Israel, Saudi Arabia and Turkey where victims were identified [S3].

provenance.importedSummary: Ababil of Minab is an emerging pro-Iranian hacktivist group with a limited public profile and little verifiable prior activity in threat intelligence reporting. The group claims responsibility for a cyberattack and allegedly possesses administrative access to targeted systems. Their pro-Iran messaging and targeting of a major US public transit authority align with known patterns of Iranian-aligned actors targeting US critical infrastructure. The use of escalatory language suggests potential for further activity.
